## Exercise Introduction

***

### Voluntary R&D Disclosure under Asymmetric Information

Author: Niklas Lieb

***

Welcome to this problem set, which is part of my bachelor's thesis at Ulm University. It was created using the package `RTutor` by Sebastian Kranz. This interactive problem set is based on the paper **"Asymmetric Information and R&D Disclosure: Evidence from Scientific Publications"** by Baruffaldi, Simeth, and Wehrheim (Management Science, 2024). The article, appendix, and data can be found [here](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2023.4721). For brevity, this paper will simply be referred to as *the paper* and its authors as *the authors* throughout the problem set.

***

Earlier work argues that information asymmetry in financial markets can lead to an increase in the cost of capital or even prevent firms from accessing external financing altogether (Merton, 1987; Diamond & Verrecchia, 1991). One way firms may attempt to reduce these asymmetries is voluntary disclosure, such as management forecasts (Balakrishnan et al., 2014).
However, the situation is more complex for R&D-intensive firms, as the capital-market benefits of increased transparency may be partially or fully offset by the risk of proprietary information leakage to competitors (Bhattacharya & Ritter, 1983).

To study this trade-off empirically, the authors exploit mergers and closures of brokerage houses as plausibly exogenous reductions in analyst coverage. Analysts act as information intermediaries, and such coverage losses have been shown to increase information asymmetry and to depress stock prices (Hong & Kacperczyk, 2010; Kelly & Ljungqvist, 2012). The authors expect firms to counter the resulting increase in information asymmetry by disclosing more of their scientific research, and they test this by comparing affected firms with unaffected ones in a Difference-in-Differences (DiD) design.

The following figure summarizes the underlying mechanism.

<p align="center">
<img src="disclosure_tradeoff.png" style="width:90%;">
</p>
<p align="center"><em>Figure 1: The R&D disclosure trade-off. Source: own illustration based on the paper.</em></p>

***

The analysis proceeds in four steps. It starts with a first look at the data, develops the DiD estimator from a single event to the full sample, checks its robustness on a matched sample, and ends with a heterogeneity analysis that asks which firms react most strongly.

### Beginner's guide

The following paragraphs walk you through the most important elements of `RTutor`. While each exercise is self-contained and can in principle be tackled on its own, working through them in order is strongly recommended, as later exercises build on concepts introduced earlier.

- **Code Chunks:** They appear whenever R code needs to be written or completed. Each chunk is accompanied by a task description. Read it carefully before typing, as the solution is only accepted if it matches exactly what is asked for.
    + `edit`: In most cases you can start typing right away. In some cases, for example if you have not completed a previous optional task, you may first need to click this button before you can modify the code.
    + `check`: Runs the code and checks your solution.
    + `hint`: Shows an automated hint that points you in the right direction.
    + `solution`: Reveals the sample solution for the current task.
    + `data`: Displays the data used in the task.
    + `run chunk`: Runs the code without checking whether it is correct.
    + `original code`: Restores the original code if you have accidentally overwritten part of the chunk.

- **Info Boxes:** They contain additional background information and detailed explanations and can be opened by clicking on them.

- **Awards:** You receive them when you successfully complete tasks.

- **Quizzes:** They help you better understand the data and regression results.


Once you have finished an exercise, click `Go to next exercise...` to continue.


## Exercise 1 -- Overview of Data 

Before we begin the analysis, let us take a look at the underlying data, which come from several sources. Scientific publication data are obtained from [Elsevier's Scopus database](https://www.elsevier.com/products/scopus), which contains detailed records on peer-reviewed journal articles and conference proceedings. Each publication includes information on authors and their institutional affiliations, which allows the identification of firm-level scientific output. Analyst coverage data come from the [Institutional Brokers' Estimate System (I/B/E/S)](https://www.lseg.com/en/data-analytics/financial-data/company-data/ibes-estimates), a widely used database tracking earnings estimates by financial analysts. Financial and accounting information is drawn from [Compustat](https://www.marketplace.spglobal.com/en/datasets/compustat-financials-(8)) and the [Center for Research in Security Prices (CRSP)](https://www.crsp.org/). Additional sources include [Thomson's 13F database](https://wrds-www.wharton.upenn.edu/pages/get-data/thomson-reuters/) for institutional ownership data and patent data from Stoffman et al. (2022).

The sample covers U.S. publicly traded firms that are active in R&D, defined as having at least one patent and at least one year of positive R&D spending during the sample period. The treatment sample consists of 760 firms affected by 43 brokerage merger and closure events, while the control sample comprises all remaining R&D-active firms in the Compustat/CRSP universe that were not covered by the relevant brokers.

## Exercise 1.1 -- Load and Explore Data

The authors have made several datasets available for replication, all provided in Stata format (`.dta`). For this problem set, these datasets have been reduced to the variables relevant for our analysis, so that each exercise works with a focused set of columns. We first need to import the data into our environment. Fortunately, the `haven` package makes that straightforward by offering the `read_dta()` function, which reads `.dta` files and converts them into a standard R data frame. The info box below gives a brief introduction to the package and its usage.

#< info "Loading Stata files in R with read_dta()"
The `haven` package allows you to import file formats from other statistical software packages (Stata, SPSS, SAS) into R. The main function we need is `read_dta()`.

```{r "info_readdta", eval=FALSE}
# Load package
library(haven)

# Import file and store it in a variable
dat <- read_dta("filename.dta")
```

The file path is passed as a character string (in quotation marks). If the file is located in the working directory, the file name alone is sufficient. More information can be found in the [haven documentation](https://haven.tidyverse.org/).

Packages can be installed in RStudio with `install.packages()` and then loaded with `library()`. In this problem set, all required packages are already installed, so you only need to load them with `library()`.

**Identifiers**

#< quiz "quiz_row_id"
question: Think about which columns are needed together to uniquely identify a single row in the dataset.
mc:
  - FIRM_ID*
  - FYEAR*
  - E_ID*
  
success: Correct! Only the combination of `FIRM_ID`, `FYEAR`, and `E_ID` identifies a row uniquely. No single one of them is enough on its own.
failure: Not quite. Think about what would happen if two of these were the same. Could there still be more than one row?
#>

The reason all three identifiers are required becomes clear once we look at what each of them captures:

- `FIRM_ID` uniquely identifies each company in the sample.
- `FYEAR` records the fiscal year of the observation, so the same firm appears in several rows across time.
- `E_ID` links the observation to a specific brokerage merger or closure event. A firm can be affected by more than one event over the sample period and may even serve as a treated firm for one event and as a control firm for another. The same firm and year can therefore appear more than once, each time attached to a different event.

**Scientific output**

Another column worth a closer look is `PUB`. It contains the number of scientific publications in academic journals attributed to a firm in a given year. The authors focus on journal publications because a large share of firms' R&D output is disclosed this way, and such publications both reflect R&D productivity and signal a firm's research capabilities through peer review and journal rankings (Dasgupta & David, 1994).

For the empirical analysis, however, the authors do not work with this raw count directly. Instead, they use the transformed variable `LN_PUB`, which serves as the main dependent variable throughout this problem set.

#< quiz "quiz_lnpub_transform"
question: Look again at the `head()` output above and compare the columns `PUB` and `LN_PUB`. How was `LN_PUB` obtained from `PUB`?
sc:
  - By taking the natural logarithm of PUB directly, that is ln(PUB)
  - By taking the natural logarithm of one plus PUB, that is ln(1 + PUB)*
  - By taking the natural logarithm of PUB minus one, that is ln(PUB - 1)
success: Correct! `LN_PUB` is defined as ln(1 + `PUB`). Adding one before taking the logarithm keeps the transformation well defined even when a firm has zero publications.
failure: Compare the rows carefully. In several rows `PUB` equals 0 while `LN_PUB` is also 0. Plain ln(0) is undefined, so the transformation must add something to PUB before taking the logarithm.
#>

**Information asymmetry**

The authors define information asymmetry as differences in information among investors. This covers both how much individual investors know about a firm and what fraction of investors know about it at all.

Two variables in the dataset speak directly to this concept. The first is `BASPRD`, the bid-ask spread, computed as the average daily difference between the ask and bid prices, scaled by their midpoint. It is a typical proxy for information asymmetry (Kelly & Ljungqvist, 2012). The second is `COV`, the number of financial analysts issuing earnings forecasts for the firm in a given year.

The remaining variables are **control variables** and are explained in the following info box:

#< info "Control variables"
When selecting control variables, the authors follow prior studies on the relation between analyst coverage and R&D outcomes that have developed a standard vector of firm and industry characteristics (He & Tian, 2013; Guo et al., 2019).

- `LN_AT`: firm size, measured by the natural logarithm of total assets

- `RDTA`: investment in R&D, measured by R&D expenditures scaled by total assets

- `LN_AGE`: firm age, measured by the natural logarithm of the number of years the firm is listed on CRSP/Compustat

- `PPETA`: asset tangibility, measured by net property, plant, and equipment scaled by total assets

- `CAPEXTA`: investment in fixed assets, measured by capital expenditures scaled by total assets

- `ROA`: profitability, measured by return on assets

- `LEV`: leverage, measured by total debt scaled by total assets

- `Q`: growth opportunities, measured by Tobin's Q

- `DELAYCON`: financial constraints, measured by the Hoberg and Maksimovic (2015) text-based index

- `INSTOWN`: institutional ownership, measured by the fraction of institutional investors

- `HINDEX`: product market competition, measured 
by the Herfindahl index based on sales

- `HINDEX2`: product market competition, measured 
by the squared Herfindahl index based on sales

#>

**Compact overview**

Having gone through the variables individually, we can now look at them collectively. A good starting point for any empirical analysis is a compact overview of the entire dataset, showing how each variable is distributed, what its typical values are, and how many observations are missing.

The `skimr` package provides this. Its `skim()` function summarizes every column in a single call and presents the result in a structured form. The info box below explains its most useful output fields.

#< info "skim(): compact overviews of datasets"
The `skim()` function generates an informative summary of a dataset, similar to `summary()` but presented in a more structured and readable format. For numeric variables, it reports information such as:

- `n_missing`: number of missing values
- `complete_rate`: proportion of complete observations
- `mean`, `sd`: mean and standard deviation
- `p0`, `p25`, `p50`, `p75`, `p100`: quantiles (minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum)
- `hist`: mini histogram

```{r "info_skim", eval=FALSE}
library(skimr)
skim(dat)
```

#< quiz "quiz_pub_skew"
question: Compare the mean and the median of `PUB`, and look at the `hist` column. What does this tell you about the distribution of publications across firms?
sc:
  - Publications are roughly evenly distributed across firms
  - Most firms have few publications, while a small number have very many (right-skewed)*

## Exercise 1.2 -- Look at a Specific Event

Before turning to the formal analysis, it is worth looking at a single firm-event combination in detail. According to the authors, treated firms should increase their scientific publication output after losing analyst coverage, and this jump should be particularly pronounced between the year just before and the year just after the event.

**A concrete firm-event example**

To make this concrete, we pick one event (`E_ID == 6`) and one of the firms it affected (`FIRM_ID == 786`) and plot the firm's annual publication count around the shock. The dataset is anonymized, so these identifiers carry no names on their own. To give the pair a more tangible interpretation, we assume throughout this exercise that `E_ID == 6` corresponds to the acquisition of the brokerage house Tucker Anthony Sutro by the Royal Bank of Canada. The deal was announced in August 2001 for 625 million U.S. dollars, and Tucker Anthony Sutro was subsequently merged into the bank's Dain Rauscher brokerage (New York Times, 2001). Along the same lines, we take `FIRM_ID == 786` to be a mid-sized biotechnology firm that lost coverage in this event. Both assumptions serve illustrative purposes only.

**Slicing the dataset**

For the plot we do not need the full dataset. Two things have to happen. First, out of all firm-year rows we keep only those belonging to this one firm in this one event. Second, out of all columns we keep only the two that the plot uses, the fiscal year and the publication count. In `dplyr` these are two separate operations. `filter()` picks **rows** by a condition, and `select()` picks **columns** by name. Because the output of the first is the input of the second, we can chain them into a single readable pipeline. The info box below explains both functions and the chaining operator that connects them.

#< info "filter() and select(): subsetting rows and columns"
Both functions are the standard tools for "slicing" a dataset into the part you need.

- **`filter()`** keeps the **rows** for which a logical condition is `TRUE`. Multiple conditions separated by commas are combined with logical AND (so all conditions must hold).
- **`select()`** keeps (or drops) **columns** by name.  

The **pipe** operator `%>%` passes the result on its left as the first argument of the function on its right, so `dat %>% filter(...)` is just another way of writing `filter(dat, ...)`. Its value shows once several steps are chained. Instead of nesting calls inside one another or storing an intermediate result after every step, the pipe lets the data flow through the operations from top to bottom, in the same order they are applied. Read `%>%` as *and then*.

```{r "info_filter_select", eval=FALSE}
# Without the pipe, filter and select are nested inside out
select(filter(dat, FYEAR == 2005, FIRM_ID == 12), COV, BASPRD)
# With the pipe, the same steps read top to bottom
dat %>%
  filter(FYEAR == 2005, FIRM_ID == 12) %>%   # first keep the rows
  select(COV, BASPRD)                          # then keep the columns
```
#>

**Task:** Complete the code below so that it keeps only the rows for our biotechnology firm in the Tucker Anthony event and only the columns `PUB` and `FYEAR`. Store the result in `dat_firm_event`.


With `dat_firm_event` in shape, we can now visualize the biotechnology firm's annual publication output around the 2001 Tucker Anthony event. The package of choice is `ggplot2`, which builds plots layer by layer following the so-called *grammar of graphics*. You start with a dataset and an *aesthetic mapping* (which variable goes on which axis) and then add geometric layers (lines, points, reference lines), scales, annotations, labels, and a theme, each connected with a `+`. 
The info box below walks through every component of the plot in turn. For a deeper dive into `ggplot2`, the official documentation can be found [here](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/index.html).

#< info "Anatomy of the ggplot() call below"
| Component | What it does |
|---|---|
| `ggplot(dat_firm_event, aes(x = FYEAR, y = PUB))` | Initializes the plot. `aes()` ("aesthetic mapping") tells ggplot which variable to use on each axis. Every layer added afterward inherits this mapping unless overridden. |
| `geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.7)` | Draws a connecting line between yearly observations. `alpha` controls transparency (1 = opaque, 0 = invisible). |
| `geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#1F77B4")` | Plots the individual yearly observations as points so each data point is clearly visible on top of the line. |
| `geom_vline(xintercept = 2001, linetype = "dashed", color = "#D62728", linewidth = 0.8)` | Adds a vertical reference line at 2001, the year of the Tucker Anthony coverage shock. |
| `annotate("label", x = 2001, y = 70, label = "Coverage shock (2001)", ...)` | Places a text label next to the event line. Unlike `geom_text()`, `annotate()` is used for one-off labels that do not depend on the data. |
| `scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1998, 2004, 1))` | Controls the x-axis: shows a tick mark for every year between 1998 and 2004. |
| `labs(x = ..., y = ..., title = ..., subtitle = ...)` | Sets axis labels, the main title, and the subtitle in one call. |
| `theme_minimal(base_size = 12)` | Applies a clean, light-background theme with a default font size of 12 pt. |
| `theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), ...)` | Fine-tunes the theme: removes minor grid lines and the vertical major grid, and makes the title and axis labels bold. `element_blank()` simply means "do not draw this element". |

#>

**Task:** Fill in the aesthetic mapping. `FYEAR` belongs on the x-axis, and the publication count `PUB` on the y-axis. Then press `check`.

```{r "1_5"}
#< fill_in
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(dat_firm_event, aes(x = ___, y = ___)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#1F77B4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2001, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#D62728", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = 2001, y = 70,
    label = "Coverage shock (2001)",
    angle = 90, vjust = -0.3,
    size = 3.5, fill = "white"
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1998, 2004, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Fiscal Year",
    y = "Publications",
    title = "Publications over Time",
    subtitle = "The 2001 Tucker Anthony coverage shock"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
#>
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(dat_firm_event, aes(x = FYEAR, y = PUB)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "#2C3E50", alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2.5, color = "#1F77B4") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 2001, linetype = "dashed",
             color = "#D62728", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate(
    "label",
    x = 2001, y = 70,
    label = "Coverage shock (2001)",
    angle = 90, vjust = -0.3,
    size = 3.5, fill = "white", label.size = 0.2
  ) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(1998, 2004, 1)) +
  labs(
    x = "Fiscal Year",
    y = "Publications",
    title = "Publications over Time",
    subtitle = "The 2001 Tucker Anthony coverage shock"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.title = element_text(face = "bold")
  )
```


#< award "ggplot2 Pioneer!"
Excellent! You have assembled your first layered `ggplot2` plot, combining lines, points, a reference line, and annotations into a single figure.
#>

The picture is striking. The firm's publication output is relatively flat in the three years before the brokerage merger and rises noticeably afterward, which is the pattern the disclosure hypothesis predicts.
Of course, one firm in one event is **no** proof of causality. The rise might have nothing to do with the loss of coverage. A biotechnology firm that starts a new research program or enters a new phase in its drug development naturally produces more scientific output around the same time, and if such a shift happened to coincide with 2001, it would show up in the plot just the same. To establish whether there is a **causal effect**, we need to rule out such alternative explanations, which we will do in the following exercise.


## Exercise 2 -- Difference-in-Differences Regression

With a feel for the data in hand, we now turn to the paper's central question of whether a loss of analyst coverage causes firms to publish more. Answering a *causal* question like this is harder than it first appears, because it requires a design that isolates the shock to coverage from everything else that makes firms differ. This is the job of the **Difference-in-Differences (DiD)** approach, which this exercise builds up step by step.

- **2.1 The Limits of a Simple Regression.** We start with the most obvious approach, a plain OLS regression of publications on coverage, and use omitted variable bias and a causal graph to see why its result cannot be read causally.
- **2.2 The DiD Idea in a Single Event.** Narrowing the view to a single event, we compute the difference-in-differences by hand from four group means and show that a regression returns the same number. This exposes the core logic of the estimator and the parallel trends condition it relies on.
- **2.3 The DiD Regression on the Full Sample.** We translate the manual calculation into a fixed effects regression that handles all firms and events at once, add time-varying controls, and put the parallel trends assumption to the test in an event study.


## Exercise 2.1 -- The Limits of a Simple Regression

The most direct way to answer the question "Do firms publish more when they face higher information asymmetry?" would be to regress the number of scientific publications on the number of analysts following the firm. Let us try this. We first load the data and then run a simple OLS regression of `LN_PUB` on `COV`.

If you want a quick reminder of how to run and read an OLS regression in R, expand the box below.

#< info "OLS regression in R"

### `lm()`

The function `lm()` (*linear model*) estimates OLS regressions in R:

```{r "info_ols_lm", eval=FALSE}
# Simple regression: y on x
reg <- lm(y ~ x, data = dat)

# Multiple regression: y on x1 and x2
reg <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = dat)
```

The variable to the left of `~` is the dependent variable, and the right-hand side lists the explanatory variables. The `data` argument passes the dataset. The intercept $\beta_0$ is estimated automatically.

### `summary()`

Calling `summary(reg)` prints the full regression output. The key columns of the coefficient table are:

| Column | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Estimate` | The OLS estimate $\hat{\beta}_k$ |
| `Std. Error` | The standard error of $\hat{\beta}_k$ |
| `t value` | The t-statistic $\hat{\beta}_k \,/\, \text{se}(\hat{\beta}_k)$, which measures how many standard errors the estimate lies away from 0 |
| `Pr(>\|t\|)` | The p-value, which is the probability of obtaining a t-statistic at least as large in absolute value as the observed one if the true coefficient were 0. A small p-value therefore counts as evidence against $H_0\colon \beta_k = 0$ |

Significance stars (`*`, `**`, `***`) indicate the magnitude of the p-value. By convention, a coefficient is called **statistically significant** if its p-value is below 5%.

```{r "info_ols_summary", eval=FALSE}
summary(reg)

# Example output:
#              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
# (Intercept) 18.5163    0.6048   30.62   < 2e-16 ***
# x            0.3127    0.0915    3.42   0.000632 ***
```

#>
